roomDerivation.name: all-zero-secret
roomDerivation.note: Edge case: a room secret of all-zero bytes derives normally - HKDF has no weak inputs.

roomDerivation.name: all-0xff-secret
roomDerivation.note: Edge case: a room secret of all-0xff bytes derives normally.

roomDerivation.name: typical-secret-1
roomDerivation.note: A representative room secret, reused across the credential/roster/signal groups below so those vectors trace back to one room.

roomDerivation.name: typical-secret-2
roomDerivation.note: A second representative secret, used as "a different room" in wrong-room negative cases elsewhere.

channelDerivation.name: agents
channelDerivation.note: The `agents` channel of ROOM_1: id = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = roomKey, info = "kithmoot/v1/channel-id/agents", 32 bytes) as hex, key = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = roomKey, info = "kithmoot/v1/channel-key/agents", 32 bytes). No salt. A chat event on this channel carries the id in its `d` tag and is NIP-44-encrypted under the key; the credential inside is still checked against the ROOM id.

channelDerivation.name: transcript
channelDerivation.note: The `transcript` channel of ROOM_1: id = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = roomKey, info = "kithmoot/v1/channel-id/transcript", 32 bytes) as hex, key = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = roomKey, info = "kithmoot/v1/channel-key/transcript", 32 bytes). No salt. A chat event on this channel carries the id in its `d` tag and is NIP-44-encrypted under the key; the credential inside is still checked against the ROOM id.

channelDerivation.name: unnamed-is-the-room
channelDerivation.note: No channel name means the main chat: the id is the room id and the key is the room key, unchanged, so every chat event ever published decodes exactly as before channels existed.

joinUrl.name: basic-no-policy
joinUrl.note: The common case: a secret and two relay hints, no access policy.

joinUrl.name: kith-policy-with-admitted-issuer
joinUrl.note: A kith-gated policy round-trips its admitted-issuer allow-list.

joinUrl.name: open-policy-has-no-admitted-list
joinUrl.note: An 'open' policy carries no admitted list at all - decodeJoinUrl must not invent one.

joinUrl.name: empty-relay-list
joinUrl.note: Edge case: an empty relay list is a valid, if useless, join URL.

joinUrl.name: members-policy-round-trip
joinUrl.note: A two-member policy, the shape of a direct message, round-trips with its members list normalised to lower case. A malformed list is refused rather than dropped, because a dropped list is an open room.

joinUrl.name: decode-malformed-fragment
joinUrl.note: A fragment that is not valid base64url must be refused, not silently treated as an open room.

output.error: join URL fragment is not valid

joinUrl.name: decode-fragment-not-json
joinUrl.note: A fragment made entirely of valid base64url characters that decodes to bytes which are not valid JSON at all - the alphabet check alone is not enough; the decoded payload must actually parse.

output.error: join URL fragment is not valid

joinUrl.name: decode-payload-wrong-shape
joinUrl.note: A fragment that decodes to valid JSON of the wrong shape - no 's' secret field at all - must be refused, not treated as a room with an empty or undefined secret.

output.error: join URL carries a malformed secret

joinUrl.name: decode-secret-wrong-length
joinUrl.note: A fragment that decodes to valid JSON but carries a 16-byte secret (not 32) must be refused.

output.error: join URL carries a malformed secret

joinUrl.name: decode-policy-unknown-tier
joinUrl.note: A policy naming a tier outside open/ken/kith/kin must be refused, not silently dropped into an open room.

output.error: join URL carries an access policy at an unknown tier

deviceCredential.name: valid
deviceCredential.note: A credential signed by the participant, authorising one device, in one room, until an expiry.

deviceCredential.name: wrong-room
deviceCredential.note: The same, valid credential, checked against a different room id than the one it names.

deviceCredential.name: expired
deviceCredential.note: A credential whose expiry has already passed at verification time.

deviceCredential.name: tampered-signature
deviceCredential.note: The valid credential's device tag swapped for a different pubkey after signing - the signature no longer covers the tags it is checked against.

rosterEvent.name: valid
rosterEvent.note: A roster entry (with its device credential nested inside) encrypted to the room key and signed by the device.

rosterEvent.name: wrong-room-key
rosterEvent.note: The same event, decrypted with room 2's key instead of the room it was actually published to - NIP-44 decryption fails its MAC check and the decoder must return null, not throw.

rosterEvent.name: wrong-signing-device
rosterEvent.note: The entry names DEVICE_A as the authorised device, but a different device (holding no credential for this room) signed the event.

rosterEvent.name: tampered-outer-signature
rosterEvent.note: The valid roster event above with its own signature corrupted - id, pubkey, tags and content untouched. Decryption, the room match, and the entry.device === event.pubkey check would all still pass; only verifying the event's own signature catches this.

rosterEvent.name: forged-credential-signature
rosterEvent.note: The outer event is genuinely signed by DEVICE_IMPOSTOR, and entry.device matches it, but the nested credential (claiming PARTICIPANT_A authorised DEVICE_IMPOSTOR) is the valid DEVICE_A credential with its device tag swapped after signing - PARTICIPANT_A never signed this. Room, decrypt, the outer signature, and entry.device === event.pubkey all pass; only verifying the nested credential's own signature catches this.

rosterEvent.name: display-name
rosterEvent.note: A roster entry carrying an ordinary display name. The name is inside the room-key ciphertext, alongside the participant pubkey and the credential - a relay that could read the guest list by name would be worse than one that could read it by pubkey, not better. The name survives the round trip exactly as typed, and decides nothing: `participant` and the nested credential are still what say who this is.

rosterEvent.name: display-name-hostile
rosterEvent.note: A genuine, fully valid roster entry whose display name carries a right-to-left override, a smuggled newline, a zero-width space and 200 characters of padding - published by a client that sanitised nothing. The entry is ACCEPTED (the person and their credential are genuine) and the name is neutralised: every Unicode 'other' character removed, whitespace collapsed, and the result capped at 32 code points. `expected.result.name` is what a reader must end up with.

rosterEvent.name: farewell
rosterEvent.note: The entry a device publishes as it leaves: empty tracks and claims, `reply: true` so nobody answers it, and `left: true` so every other device removes it at once instead of waiting out the presence timeout. A reader that does not know `left` treats this as an ordinary answer carrying nothing and evicts the device on the timeout. Only a JSON `true` is a farewell; any other value is not one.

rosterEvent.name: agent
rosterEvent.note: A roster entry from a device declaring itself an automated participant with `agent: true`. Inside the room-key ciphertext like everything else. A reader keeps the flag; a member may use it to decide what media this device is sent. A reader that does not know the field sees an ordinary entry.

rosterEvent.name: agent-loose-value
rosterEvent.note: A genuine roster entry whose `agent` field is the string "yes" rather than the JSON boolean `true`. The entry is ACCEPTED and the field is DROPPED: only an honest `true` declares an agent, because the flag decides what a member sends this device. `expected.result` carries no `agent` at all.

rosterEvent.name: assist-offer
rosterEvent.note: A roster entry carrying an offer to relay for the room: measured reachability, the uplink estimate every client derives spare capacity from, and how many pairs this device is already carrying. It is inside the room-key ciphertext with everything else - a relay that could read which members were publicly reachable and how much bandwidth they had would be reading a map of the room. The offer survives the round trip exactly as published, and decides nothing on its own: what it feeds is a selection every client computes independently from the same roster.

rosterEvent.name: assist-offer-hostile
rosterEvent.note: A genuine, fully valid roster entry whose assist offer is nonsense: a null uplink, a negative peer count, a fractional load, a claim to carry five thousand pairs, and a reachability that is not one of the four measured answers. The entry is ACCEPTED and the offer is dropped whole - `expected.result` carries no `assist` field at all. Repairing it would be worse than dropping it: a mended number is still a number the publisher chose, and it would go on to decide who carries this room.

signalWrap.name: offer
signalWrap.note: An SDP offer, gift-wrapped so the relay sees neither the SDP nor the sender's identity - only that someone sent something to the recipient.

signalWrap.name: ice-candidate
signalWrap.note: A trickled ICE candidate, wrapped the same way as an offer or answer.

signalWrap.name: wrong-recipient
signalWrap.note: The offer wrap above, opened by someone other than the intended recipient - the ECDH shared point differs, so the outer NIP-44 payload fails to authenticate and unwrapSignal must return null.

signalWrap.name: wrong-room
signalWrap.note: The offer wrap above, unwrapped correctly by the real recipient but checked against a room id the inner body does not name.

signalWrap.name: tampered-inner-signature
signalWrap.note: The offer's inner event with its own signature corrupted - id, pubkey, tags and content untouched - re-wrapped under a fresh (but otherwise ordinary) ephemeral key. The outer wrap decrypts fine, and inner.kind, body.roomId, and the addressed 'p' tag all still check out; only verifying the inner event's own signature catches this.

kindredProof.name: ken
kindredProof.note: A ken proof: the issuer vouches for GUEST at the 'ken' tier, in ROOM_1, until KINDRED_EXPIRES_AT. The room and the nonce are both inside the signed message - see canonicalMessage in src/access.ts - so a proof cannot be edited into another room, and two proofs on identical terms are still distinguishable. Pins the signed message layout, not any admission decision - see the accessEvaluation group for that.

kindredProof.name: kith
kindredProof.note: A kith proof: the issuer vouches for GUEST at the 'kith' tier, in ROOM_1, until KINDRED_EXPIRES_AT. The room and the nonce are both inside the signed message - see canonicalMessage in src/access.ts - so a proof cannot be edited into another room, and two proofs on identical terms are still distinguishable. Pins the signed message layout, not any admission decision - see the accessEvaluation group for that.

kindredProof.name: kin
kindredProof.note: A kin proof: the issuer vouches for GUEST at the 'kin' tier, in ROOM_1, until KINDRED_EXPIRES_AT. The room and the nonce are both inside the signed message - see canonicalMessage in src/access.ts - so a proof cannot be edited into another room, and two proofs on identical terms are still distinguishable. Pins the signed message layout, not any admission decision - see the accessEvaluation group for that.

accessEvaluation.name: open-room-admits-anyone
accessEvaluation.note: An open room admits any participant without a proof at all.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-admits-kith-proof
accessEvaluation.note: A kith-gated room admits a matching kith proof from a trusted issuer.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-admits-kin-proof
accessEvaluation.note: A kith-gated room also admits a kin proof - kin is closer than kith.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-rejects-ken-proof
accessEvaluation.note: A kith-gated room refuses a ken proof - ken is one-way recognition and never satisfies a kith gate ('tier too low').

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-rejects-untrusted-issuer
accessEvaluation.note: A kith-gated room refuses a well-formed, correctly-signed kith proof from an issuer not on its allow-list.

accessEvaluation.name: members-admit-a-listed-participant
accessEvaluation.note: An open room with a members list admits a participant on the list, with no proof, as an open room does.

accessEvaluation.name: members-refuse-a-stranger
accessEvaluation.note: A members list shuts the door to anybody not on it, whatever the tier says ('not a member'). This is what makes a two-member room a direct message.

accessEvaluation.name: members-compared-case-insensitively
accessEvaluation.note: A members entry in upper-case hex names the same participant. The rule every hex identifier here follows.

accessEvaluation.name: members-still-need-the-tier
accessEvaluation.note: A listed member of a kith-gated room still needs a kith proof ('no kindred proof'): the list narrows who may enter, it never widens what they must show.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-admits-issuer-via-upper-case-allow-list-entry
accessEvaluation.note: The allow-list names the trusted issuer (HOST) in upper-case hex; the proof itself is issued and signed normally, so its issuer field is the ordinary lower-case pubkey. Still admitted - an implementation that compares the allow-list entry to the issuer with an exact string match wrongly refuses this.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-admits-upper-case-issuer-against-lower-case-allow-list
accessEvaluation.note: The mirror image: the proof carries its own issuer field in upper-case hex - issuer is not part of the signed message (see canonicalMessage in src/access.ts), so upper-casing it does not disturb the signature - while the room's allow-list names HOST in the ordinary lower case. Still admitted.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-rejects-proof-for-another-room
accessEvaluation.note: A kith proof from the trusted issuer, at a sufficient tier, unexpired, naming the right participant - and minted for a different room. An implementation that does not compare proof.room to the room being joined admits a proof its issuer never granted here ('proof names another room').

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-rejects-room-edited-into-the-proof
accessEvaluation.note: The same other-room proof with its `room` field rewritten to name this room. The room is inside the signed message, so rewriting it invalidates the signature ('bad signature') - an implementation that binds the room but leaves it out of canonicalMessage admits this.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-admits-proof-against-upper-case-room-id
accessEvaluation.note: The room id handed to evaluateAccess is upper-case hex naming the very room the proof was minted for. Hex identifiers are compared case-insensitively throughout - see the section of this README on that - so this is still admitted.

accessEvaluation.name: kith-room-rejects-tampered-signature
accessEvaluation.note: A kith proof from the trusted issuer, at a sufficient tier, unexpired, naming the right participant - identical to 'kith-room-admits-kith-proof' except its signature is garbage. Every check before the final schnorr verification passes; skip that check, or skip it entirely, and this is indistinguishable from a genuine proof.

turnCredential.name: coturn-known-vector
turnCredential.note: Cross-checked independently with Node's own crypto module (see src/turn.test.ts) - HMAC-SHA1('my-shared-secret', '1735776000:kithmoot') base64-encoded.

turnCredential.name: custom-device-name
turnCredential.note: A per-viewer name in place of the default.

turnCredential.name: fractional-seconds-floor
turnCredential.note: ttl and now are floored before being summed, so expiry is always a whole Unix second.

turnCredential.name: zero-ttl
turnCredential.note: Edge case: a zero-length TTL still mints a credential that expires immediately.

roomDescriptor.name: no-forwarders
roomDescriptor.note: A room that names no forwarder at all - the ordinary case for a small mesh. The empty list is explicit on the wire, not an absent field, so a reader never has to guess whether the room has forwarders or the publisher forgot to say.

roomDescriptor.name: one-forwarder
roomDescriptor.note: One forwarder, named by url and pubkey. The pubkey is the forwarder's own Nostr key - it identifies the forwarder, and grants it nothing.

roomDescriptor.name: several-forwarders
roomDescriptor.note: Three forwarders with different fields present: url+pubkey, url+label, url alone. All three fields except url are optional and an absent one must stay absent, not become an empty string or a null.

roomDescriptor.name: forwarder-extra-fields-stripped
roomDescriptor.note: The descriptor decodes, but the forwarder entry does not survive intact: a conforming decoder projects each entry onto url/pubkey/label, so the roomKey and note fields this one carries are dropped. A decoder that passes the JSON object through instead will return them, and will have handed a forwarder reference the room key.

roomDescriptor.name: wrong-room-key
roomDescriptor.note: The one-forwarder descriptor decrypted with room 2's key - NIP-44's MAC check fails and the decoder must return null, not throw. A relay, or a forwarder, holds neither key and so learns nothing from either.

roomDescriptor.name: wrong-signing-device
roomDescriptor.note: A descriptor naming DEVICE_A, correctly encrypted to the room key, but signed by a device holding no credential for this room - a member repointing the room at its own forwarder under somebody else's name. Holding the room key is not authority to rewrite the room's config; the credential is.

roomEpoch.name: epoch-zero-is-the-room
roomEpoch.note: Epoch 0 is not a special case bolted on: it derives to exactly what `deriveRoom` derives, with the same two HKDF info strings and no salt. A client that has never heard of epochs and one that has agree byte for byte on a room nobody has been removed from, which is what makes the whole mechanism additive.

roomEpoch.name: epoch-one
roomEpoch.note: The first successor. `id = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = secret, info = "kithmoot/v1/epoch-id/1", 32)` as hex and `key = HKDF-SHA256(ikm = secret, info = "kithmoot/v1/epoch-key/1", 32)`, no salt. The secret is the one the rekey sealed to each remaining device - NOT the original room secret, which the removed device still holds and which now opens nothing.

roomEpoch.name: epoch-two
roomEpoch.note: A second removal from a room already at epoch 1: a fresh secret again, and the info strings carry the number so two epochs of one room never collide.

roomEpoch.name: rekey
roomEpoch.note: The authority moves the room to epoch 1 and removes one device. Encrypted to the epoch being LEFT, so everybody currently in the room can read who left; the successor secret inside is sealed separately to each device that stays, under a NIP-44 conversation key between the authority and that device, so the removed device reads the notice and not the secret. `peekRekeyEvent` answers "which epoch is this" with no key at all, which is how a device that has fallen behind knows it has.

roomEpoch.name: rekey-read-by-the-removed-device
roomEpoch.note: The same event, decoded by the device it removes. It decodes - the notice is encrypted to the epoch that device still holds - and it carries no `secret`, because no copy was sealed to it. A client must treat "decoded, no secret" as "you are out", not as an error: it is how a removed member learns it has been removed, and it is the only notice it will get.

roomEpoch.name: rekey-closed
roomEpoch.note: Closing a room is a rekey with no sealed copies at all: the epoch advances and nobody is given the successor, so nothing further can be published or read. `closed` is inside the ciphertext and is only a JSON `true`; the empty `keys` object is what actually closes the room, and a client that ignored the flag would still find itself with no key.

roomEpoch.name: rekey-not-the-authority
roomEpoch.note: A perfectly formed rekey, correctly encrypted to the current epoch, signed by a member who is not the room authority - which is to say, by anybody else who holds the room key, which is everybody in the room. It is REFUSED before decryption, on the signing key alone. Without this check any member could remove any other, and "removal" would mean nothing.

roomEpoch.name: rekey-skips-an-epoch
roomEpoch.note: The authority naming epoch 3 while this device is at epoch 0. Refused: only the very next epoch is applied, so a device cannot be walked forward past a removal it never saw, and a replayed rekey from an epoch already passed cannot move it backwards either. `peekRekeyEvent` still answers 3, which is how a client knows it is behind and should ask.

roomEpoch.name: admins-signature
roomEpoch.note: Who may remove somebody, said by the authority and checkable by everybody. The message is `sha256("kithmoot/v1/admins:<roomId>:<epoch>:<admins joined by comma>")` over the CANONICAL list - lower-cased, deduplicated, sorted - so two clients that hold the same set in different orders verify the same signature. The epoch is inside the message, so a list signed for one epoch does not authorise anybody after the next removal.

roomEpoch.name: admins-signature-another-epoch
roomEpoch.note: The same signature, offered for epoch 2. Refused: a list is authorised for the epoch it names and no other, so an admin set from before a removal cannot be replayed to re-authorise somebody after it.

agentOwnership.name: valid
agentOwnership.note: The smallest honest proof: an agent pubkey, a principal pubkey, when it was issued, and a BIP-340 signature over `sha256("kithmoot/v1/agent-owner:<agent>:<principal>:<issuedAt>:<expiresAt>:<label>")`. Note the two empty fields: an absent expiry and an absent label are the EMPTY STRING in the signed message, not omitted, so a proof with no expiry and one whose expiry is the empty string cannot be made to collide.

agentOwnership.name: with-expiry-and-label
agentOwnership.note: The same proof with a horizon and a human label. The label is sanitised BEFORE it is signed, so what a reader renders is what the principal actually put their name to - and a reader must re-sanitise and compare, which is the `label-not-as-signed` negative below.

agentOwnership.name: names-another-agent
agentOwnership.note: A genuine, correctly signed proof presented for a DIFFERENT agent - the exact move an agent would make to borrow somebody else standing. The check is against the agent whose roster entry or chat message carries it, never against the agent named inside, so the proof is refused with `names another agent`.

agentOwnership.name: expired
agentOwnership.note: Signed properly and out of date. Expiry is the only revocation this proof has, so it is checked strictly: `expiresAt <= now` is expired, not "expired a moment ago is fine".

agentOwnership.name: label-not-as-signed
agentOwnership.note: A label carrying a right-to-left override, signed exactly as written. The signature verifies; the proof does not. A reader sanitises the label and refuses when the result differs from what was signed, because otherwise a principal could sign one thing and every reader would render another. `label is not as signed` is the reason.

agentOwnership.name: its-own-principal
agentOwnership.note: An agent signing for itself, which is a valid signature over a meaningless claim: the whole point of the proof is that somebody ELSE vouched. Refused on the two keys being equal, before the signature is even checked.

result.reason: an agent cannot be its own principal

agentOwnership.name: bad-signature
agentOwnership.note: Every field right and the signature wrong. Checked last, because it is the expensive one, but checked.

agentOwnership.name: normalised-shape
agentOwnership.note: What a reader must make of an ownership proof off the wire before it verifies anything: keys lower-cased, unknown fields dropped, and the surviving fields written back in a fixed order - `agent, principal, issuedAt, sig, expiresAt, label`. This is the order the roster and chat encoders re-serialise, so an implementation that keeps the sender order produces different bytes for the same proof.

chatAttachment.name: chat-with-attachment
chatAttachment.note: One share on one message. Everything that matters is inside the ciphertext: a relay carrying this sees a chat event for a room id and nothing about a file, and the Blossom server that holds the bytes sees a hash being fetched and never the key. `name`, `type` and `size` are the sender's hints for rendering before the envelope is opened; the envelope carries its own metadata and that is the authority.

chatAttachment.name: attachments-a-reader-must-defuse
chatAttachment.note: Three attachments from a client that checked nothing. The first is served over plain HTTP and is DROPPED - a share is https or it is not a share, because the URL is fetched by the browser and a downgrade is a downgrade. The second has a key that is not 32 bytes of hex and is dropped. The third survives with its name defused (the right-to-left override goes), its media type lower-cased, and its non-integer size dropped. The MESSAGE is kept throughout: a bad attachment costs the attachment, never the sentence somebody wrote.

result.text: two of these are not shares
two of these are not shares

chatAttachment.name: more-attachments-than-a-message-may-carry
chatAttachment.note: Five shares on one message. The WHOLE MESSAGE is refused rather than the extras being trimmed, and the count is taken as sent rather than after filtering: a cap that silently truncates is a cap an attacker tunes, and one that counts survivors can be walked past with junk entries.

chatAttachment.name: envelope-key-derivation
chatAttachment.note: The recovery key in the chat is not the AES key: the AES key is `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = recovery key, salt = the envelope header salt, info = "forgesworn-aes-256-gcm-chunked/v2", 32)`. The salt is in the header of the envelope being opened, so the same recovery key opens exactly one envelope and knowing it tells you nothing about another.

chatAttachment.name: padded-plaintext-length
chatAttachment.note: What an envelope's length is allowed to say about the file inside it. Everything up to 64 KiB is padded to 64 KiB; up to a mebibyte, to the next power of two; beyond that, to the next whole mebibyte. A watcher who can see only the size of an upload therefore learns a bucket rather than a fingerprint.

chatAttachment.name: file-event
chatAttachment.note: The NIP-94 kind-1063 event that announces a sealed envelope: tags in a fixed order, `x` and `ox` both the hash of the served bytes, the media type the opaque envelope type rather than the file's own, and an `alt` that says nothing about the contents. Deterministic given the url, hash, size and time, so two implementations announcing the same upload produce the same event.

chatAttachment.name: upload-authorisation
chatAttachment.note: The kind-24242 Blossom authorisation an uploader signs: bound to one hash and one server, expiring ninety seconds later, and stamped a second early so a server whose clock is a moment behind does not refuse a fresh one.

approvalControl.name: approval-request
approvalControl.note: A question, its options and its horizon. The id is what an answer refers to; the options are what an answer may say, exactly, case-sensitively. Encoded as JSON in the text of a chat message on the `control` channel, so everybody in the room can read both the question and every answer to it - an agent asking permission in private would not be asking permission.

message.text: Publish the minutes to the town hall room?

output.text: {"op":"approval-request","id":"spend-1","text":"Publish the minutes to the town hall room?","options":["approve","decline"],"expiresAt":1800000600}

result.text: Publish the minutes to the town hall room?

approvalControl.name: approval-request-without-options
approvalControl.note: Options are optional on the wire; a reader keeps the message as sent, with no options field. The default pair - approve and decline - is applied by the agent that asked, not by the decoder, so a decoder never invents an option the asker did not offer.

approvalControl.name: approval
approvalControl.note: An answer names the question it answers and says one of its options. Nothing here says who answered: that is the chat message's participant, bound to a device credential, which is the only attribution that cannot be typed by somebody else.

approvalControl.name: approval-request-duplicate-options
approvalControl.note: Repeated options are deduplicated in the order they were first offered, and NOT sorted or lower-cased: an option list is a menu a person reads, so the order is the asker's and the comparison against a verdict is exact.

approvalControl.name: approval-verdict-with-a-newline
approvalControl.note: A verdict carrying a newline, which a renderer might show as one word and a comparison might treat as another. Refused whole: a verdict is a short token from a fixed alphabet, and anything else is not an answer.

approvalControl.name: approval-request-option-list-too-long
approvalControl.note: Nine options where eight is the cap. Refused whole rather than trimmed, for the same reason the attachment cap refuses the message: a limit that silently drops the tail is a limit an attacker aims at.

approvalControl.name: approval-request-id-that-is-a-path
approvalControl.note: An id is a short token, not a name a reader might resolve against anything. Refused.

approvalControl.name: not-a-control-message
approvalControl.note: Somebody typing into the control channel by hand. It is a perfectly good chat message and not a control message, and a reader must treat it as the former: the channel is a place in the room, and people can write there.

approvalControl.name: admins-announcement
approvalControl.note: Who may answer an approval, announced on the same channel. ANY member may publish this op - the channel is the room's - and only the authority's signature over the canonical list makes it believed, which is what the `roomEpoch/admins-signature` vector pins. A reader that took the list on the word of whoever sent it would let any member appoint themselves.

verificationWords.name: pair-a-b
verificationWords.note: The reference pair. Each side gets three space-separated words from the spoken-token wordlist; the two sides differ, so the second speaker cannot pass by repeating the first.

verificationWords.name: pair-b-a-same-as-a-b
verificationWords.note: The same pair, given the other way round. Both clients sort the keys, so the output is identical to `pair-a-b` - neither side has to agree who goes first.

verificationWords.name: pair-a-c-differs-from-a-b
verificationWords.note: A's words against C, which must NOT equal A's words against B. An implementation that derives from the speaker alone gives A one word for everybody and passes against an impostor standing in for anyone.

verificationWords.name: pair-a-b-other-room
verificationWords.note: The same pair under a different room key. The words move with the room, which is what makes an epoch rekey change them.

verificationWords.name: same-participant-refused
verificationWords.note: A participant cannot verify against itself. There is no honest answer, and returning a plausible-looking word would put something on screen that proves nothing.

verificationWords.name: short-room-key-refused
verificationWords.note: The room key is 32 bytes. Anything else is a caller error, not something to derive from.

chatThread.name: reply-to-root
chatThread.note: B answers A. A reply to a root carries `reply` and `thread`, equal, each naming the target by id AND author: an id is chosen by its sender, so an id alone is anybody's to reuse. The reader nests the reply under the root and the main stream shows one message.

results.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

replies.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

chatThread.name: reply-deeper-in-a-thread
chatThread.note: A answers B's reply. `thread` still names the root; `reply` names the message answered. Both replies sit under the root, in time order, and the second records which message it answered.

results.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

replies.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

chatThread.name: reply-with-no-thread-field
chatThread.note: A reply that names only a parent: the parent is the root. Walked up through loaded messages, so a reply to a reply with no `thread` still lands under the top of the thread.

chatThread.name: reply-to-a-root-not-loaded
chatThread.note: A reply whose root this reader does not hold. The reference is kept, the message stays in the main stream marked `orphan`, and it moves under the root when the root arrives. Nothing somebody said disappears because the message it answered is older than the window.

chatThread.name: malformed-reference-dropped
chatThread.note: A `reply` that does not check out - here the author is not a key - is dropped and the message stays, which is exactly what an older client shows. The decoded message carries no `reply` and no `thread`.

chatThread.name: reply-beside-a-reaction-refused
chatThread.note: A reaction is not a message and cannot answer one. A payload carrying both is refused whole; the check is on the keys as they arrived.

chatEdit.name: edit
chatEdit.note: A replaces its own message. `replaces` names the ORIGINAL's id; the author is the message's own participant, so same-author is structural. The reader shows the edit's text on the original's frame - id, sender, time, place - marks it edited, and keeps the chain.

chatEdit.name: edit-latest-wins
chatEdit.note: Two edits of one message in the same second: the greater id wins, exactly as reactions resolve. The winning edit's mentions replace the original's.

results.text: Shall we ship on Thursday, early?

conversation.text: Shall we ship on Thursday, early?

chatEdit.name: edit-of-an-edit-lands-on-the-original
chatEdit.note: An edit that names an earlier edit rather than the original is read as naming that edit's original, so a client that got the rule wrong still converges.

chatEdit.name: edit-by-somebody-else-ignored
chatEdit.note: B "edits" A's message. It decodes - it is a well-formed message from B - but it names a message B never sent, so the original is untouched and B's edit stands as its own message, marked edited. Nobody puts words in anyone else's mouth.

chatEdit.name: edit-of-a-message-not-loaded
chatEdit.note: An edit whose original this reader does not hold stands in for it, marked edited: a correction is still something somebody said.

results.text: corrected, original older than the window

conversation.text: corrected, original older than the window

chatEdit.name: edit-naming-nothing-refused
chatEdit.note: An edit with an empty `replaces` is refused whole. Shown as a message it would duplicate what it meant to replace.

chatEdit.name: edit-with-a-thread-refused
chatEdit.note: An edit keeps the original's place in a thread and its kind; one that carries `reply`, `thread` or `kind` of its own is refused.

chatRetract.name: retract
chatRetract.note: A retracts its own message. The original and every edit of it are shown as one retracted placeholder, whatever their times: here the edit was sent AFTER the retraction and is still hidden. Once retracted, always retracted. Cooperative, like every deletion here: every admitted device already holds the plaintext.

chatRetract.name: retract-keeps-replies
chatRetract.note: Replies to a retracted root stay under it. The root shows as retracted; what people said in answer is theirs.

results.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

replies.text: Yes, if the vectors are green

chatRetract.name: retract-by-somebody-else-ignored
chatRetract.note: B "retracts" A's message. It decodes and does nothing: the tombstone names a message B never sent. A reader never shows a retraction as a message either; it is a statement, not conversation.

chatRetract.name: retract-with-attachments-refused
chatRetract.note: A retraction carries nothing else. One with attachments, mentions, a reference or a kind is refused whole.

chatMention.name: mentions-on-the-wire
chatMention.note: The sender names who this addresses: Rowan by key, and everyone. What lights up as a mention is exactly what an agent answers to, because both read this field. `everyone` addresses a person and not an agent: Tally as a person is addressed, Tally as an agent is not.

result.text: @Rowan and everyone: the vectors are green

chatMention.name: mentions-by-name-when-the-field-is-absent
chatMention.note: A message from before the field existed is read by name: a whole word in the text that matches a roster name, with or without an @. Legacy, and it goes when the wire freezes. "Rowan" is named; "Tally" is not, because "totally" is not Tally.

chatMention.name: mentions-normalised
chatMention.note: Keys lower-cased, repeats dropped, anything that is neither a key nor `everyone` dropped. The field goes altogether when nothing valid is left; here two entries survive.

chatMention.name: mentions-over-the-cap-refused
chatMention.note: More than 32 names is not something a conformant client sends, and the message is refused whole rather than trimmed.

chatInvite.name: invite
chatInvite.note: A invites B to a direct message: a room whose link admits the two of them and nobody else. The link is NIP-44 v2 between A's participant key and B's, so B opens it, and so does any other device holding A's identity - the conversation key is the same from either end - and C, holding the shared room's key and reading the message, gets null without a decrypt being tried. The text names nobody. `linkNonceHex` is the NIP-44 nonce the link was sealed with.

chatInvite.name: invite-beside-a-reaction-refused
chatInvite.note: An invitation is a statement about a room, a reaction a statement about a message; a payload carrying both is refused whole.

chatInvite.name: invite-malformed-refused
chatInvite.note: An invitation whose addressee is not a key is refused whole: there is nobody to show it to and nothing honest to show instead.

readPosition.name: read-position-id-derivation
readPosition.note: The `d` tag for a room: HKDF-SHA256 of the room's epoch-0 key with the info string `kithmoot/v1/read-position-id`, 32 bytes, hex. Every member can compute it and no relay can, so a relay cannot tie the record to a room id it carries.

readPosition.name: read-position
readPosition.note: A's read positions for one room: a kind-30078 record signed by the participant key, replaceable per room by the derived `d` tag, labelled `l: kithmoot.read.v1`, and NIP-44 v2 to A's own key. The main chat is the channel named `""`. `plaintext` is the canonical body both implementations write: channels sorted, `id` only when there is one.

readPosition.name: read-position-wrong-room-refused
readPosition.note: The same record read against another room: the `d` tag does not match that room's derived id, so it is refused before anything is decrypted.

readPosition.name: read-position-somebody-elses-refused
readPosition.note: A record expected from B and signed by A: refused on the envelope. The author is the participant key, in the clear, and a reader only ever asks for its own.

readPosition.name: read-position-without-label-refused
readPosition.note: The `l` tag is what a reader subscribes on and what says this kind-30078 record is a KithMoot read position rather than some other application's data under a colliding `d`. Without it the record is refused.

readPosition.name: read-position-merge
readPosition.note: Two devices, merged: the greater position per channel wins, `at` first and then `id`. `localAhead` says this device knew something the record did not, so it republishes; `remoteAhead` says the record moved this device on.
